<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README provided, we can see that Bililive-go is a Golang-based, multi-platform live stream recording tool with a web interface. It integrates with various live streaming services (Bilibili, Acfun, Douyu, Huya, etc.) and includes support for external monitoring tools (Grafana and Prometheus), containerized deployment (Docker/Docker Compose), and a modern web UI developed with React.

Below are the detailed guidelines for drawing an accurate system design/architecture diagram tailored to this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Live Recorder Core: This is the heart of the application. It includes the main command (src/cmd/bililive/bililive.go) that coordinates the live recording process.
   • Live Providers Integration: Represented by the modules under src/live (with subfolders for each supported streaming platform like bilibili, douyu, huya, etc.). These components handle platform-specific details.
   • Listeners & Event Handling: Under src/listeners and src/pkg/events, these modules monitor events (e.g., errors, status updates) and dispatch notifications or trigger actions.
   • Recorder Module: Under src/recorders, which manages the actual recording process by interfacing with external tools such as ffmpeg.
   • Configuration Management: Modules in src/configs (and the external config.yml/config.docker.yml files) handle runtime settings, including cookies and recording parameters.
   • Web Server & API: Found in src/servers and the web application code in src/webapp. These parts expose functionalities via HTTP endpoints for configuration management, file access, and status updates.
   • Metrics and Logging: src/metrics, src/log, and related packages capture and export monitoring data, supporting integration with Prometheus for metrics collection and Grafana for visualization.
   • Utility Libraries: Generic helper functions (src/pkg/utils, src/pkg/counter, src/pkg/reader, etc.) that support the main workflow.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   • The Application Server (HTTP server) interacts with the Webapp (React-based front end) to present configuration UIs, monitor recording statuses, and provide access to recorded videos.
   • The Recorder Core coordinates with:
       – Live Provider Modules: Each module (e.g., src/live/bilibili, src/live/douyu) implements platform-specific logic.
       – Listener Modules that capture live events, errors, and notifications.
       – The Recorder Module that uses ffmpeg (external dependency) to record streams.
   • Configuration is centrally managed and read from config files, which can be updated either manually or via the web interface.
   • Metrics and logs from the recorder modules, listeners, and server are sent out for monitoring. External systems like Prometheus and Grafana (supported via Docker-Compose configurations) retrieve, display, and alert on these metrics.
   • Docker utilization: Dockerfiles, docker-compose.yml, and related scripts indicate containerization for the service and its dependencies (e.g., the Grafana dashboard and Prometheus).

3. Highlight Important Architectural Patterns and Technologies:
   • Modular Design: The clear separation in the file structure (live modules, listeners, recorders, web server, etc.) suggests a modular architecture that can be extended with additional streaming platforms.
   • Separation of Concerns: Frontend (src/webapp) is distinct from the backend server (src/servers) and the business logic (other src subfolders).
   • Event-driven Patterns: Listeners and event dispatchers (in src/pkg/events) indicate an event-driven mechanism guiding interactions between modules.
   • Containerization and CI/CD: With Dockerfiles, docker-compose, GitHub workflows, Travis configuration, and Makefiles, the project is designed for automated builds, testing, and deployment.
   • Dependency on External Tools: ffmpeg is the key external dependency for handling media streams.

4. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • For this full-stack application, your diagram should very clearly separate the frontend (web UI) from the backend processing and recording engine. Use different colors or shapes to distinguish these two layers.
   • Clearly denote the interface/API layer that connects the web server with the underlying core services (e.g., instance managers, recorders, listeners).
   • Include external services/components such as ffmpeg (as a media processing node) and monitoring tools (Prometheus and Grafana) as part of the deployment architecture.
   • Ensure that modules dedicated to different live streaming providers are grouped under one “Live Providers” block—indicating that they share similar roles while addressing platform-specific logic.
   • Represent configuration management and logging/metrics as cross-cutting concerns affecting multiple modules.

5. Specific Elements to Include in the Diagram:
   • Use clear, well-labeled boxes for:
         - Web Interface (React front end with components and API endpoints)
         - Application Server (Golang backend handling HTTP requests and managing configuration)
         - Live Recorder Engine that contains sub-components:
              • Live Providers Modules (e.g., Bilibili, Douyu, etc.)
              • Listener/Event Dispatcher Subsystem
              • Recorder Component (integrating with ffmpeg)
         - Utility/Support Components (Configuration, Metrics, Logging)
         - Deployment & External Dependencies (Docker container environment, ffmpeg, Prometheus, Grafana)
   • Draw directional arrows to depict:
         - Data flow from the web UI to the backend server/API.
         - Event/command flow from the recorder engine to the live providers.
         - Interactions between components (e.g., configuration being read by the recorder and updated by the web UI).
         - Communication with external tools (e.g., how recorded streams are processed by ffmpeg and metrics forwarded to Prometheus).
   • Use color coding or different shapes/icons to differentiate between:
         - Core business logic modules (engine, listeners, recorders)
         - UI components (frontend webapp)
         - External services and dependencies

6. Final Advice:
   • Be very detailed: The diagram should capture all essential building blocks and their interactions. Do not hesitate to break down the system into multiple smaller diagrams if needed (e.g., one for overall architecture, one focusing on live stream processing flow, and one for deployment with Docker).
   • Include annotations or a legend: Describe each component briefly so other engineers can quickly understand the purpose of each module.
   • Emphasize modularity and separation of concerns so that new live platforms or enhancements in the web interface can be integrated into the system without major changes to the core architecture.

Following these guidelines, you’ll have a detailed and accurate system design diagram that not only reflects the structure of Bililive-go but also communicates the interactions and responsibilities of its components effectively. This will help in discussion, onboarding new developers, and planning further enhancements. 
</explanation>
